learn.hook: Your tiffin box, your chair and your bangles are all objects. But what are they made of? That's the material!
points: An object is a thing (like a spoon or a chair). A material is what it is made of (like steel, wood, plastic or glass).
One object can be made from different materials: a chair can be wooden, plastic or metal. One material can make many objects: wood makes chairs, doors and pencils.
Appearance: materials that shine, like gold, silver, copper and aluminium foil, are called lustrous. Wood, paper, cloth and chalk are non-lustrous.
Metals can lose their shine in air and moisture; a copper vessel turns dull but shines again after cleaning.
Hardness: hard materials like iron and stone are difficult to scratch or press. Soft materials like cotton and sponge can be pressed easily.

example.q: Nisha has a piece of cotton and a piece of stone. She tries to press both with her fingers. Which is hard and which is soft?
steps: The cotton gets squeezed easily when pressed.
The stone does not change at all when pressed.
A material that is easily pressed or scratched is soft; one that is not is hard.
example.answer: Stone is hard; cotton is soft.

learn.reallife: Gold and silver jewellery is loved for its lustre, and doors are made of hard wood or iron so they are strong.

quiz.q: What is the material of an object?
options: What the object is made of
quiz.explain: A material is the substance an object is made of, like wood, glass or metal.
quiz.mistake: Confuses material with shape or colour

quiz.q: Which material is lustrous?
quiz.explain: Gold has a natural shine, so it is lustrous.
quiz.mistake: Does not know what lustrous means

quiz.q: Which of these is a soft material?
quiz.explain: A sponge can be pressed easily, so it is soft.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up hard and soft

quiz.q: Why does an old copper vessel look dull?
options: Its surface has changed due to air and moisture
quiz.explain: Metals lose their shine when their surface reacts with air and moisture. Cleaning brings back the shine.
quiz.mistake: Thinks dull metals were never lustrous

quiz.q: Which object can be made from wood, plastic or metal?
quiz.explain: Chairs can be made of many materials, showing one object can be made of different materials.
quiz.mistake: Thinks each object can be made of only one material

quiz.q: Which group shows objects all made from wood?
quiz.explain: Pencils, doors and cricket bats are usually made from wood.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect objects to their common material

quiz.q: Which is a hard material?
quiz.explain: Iron is difficult to press or scratch, so it is hard.
quiz.mistake: Thinks hardness means heaviness

quiz.q: Aluminium foil is shiny. This property is called:
quiz.explain: The shine of a material is called lustre.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the names of properties

teach.ask: Gappu taps a spoon and a pencil: 'These things are made of stuff! Why do some shine and some don't? Why is one hard?'
teach.praise: Chirp! Objects are made of materials. Some materials are lustrous like gold, others dull like wood. Some are hard, some soft!
teach.nudge: What do we call a shiny material? And how can I test if something is hard or soft?

learn.hook: Sugar disappears in water, oil floats on top, and you can see through glass but not through a wall. Materials behave differently!
points: Soluble materials dissolve (mix completely) in water, like sugar and salt. Insoluble ones do not, like sand, chalk powder and sawdust.
Some liquids mix with water (lemon juice, vinegar); some do not (oil forms a layer on top).
Some objects float on water (a dry leaf, a piece of wood, a cork); others sink (a stone, an iron nail, a glass marble).
Transparent materials let us see clearly through them (clear glass, clean water, air).
Translucent materials let us see only partly (butter paper, frosted glass, oiled paper). Opaque materials do not let us see through at all (wood, cardboard, a metal sheet).

example.q: Raj adds a spoon of sand and a spoon of salt to two glasses of water and stirs. What will he see?
steps: Salt is soluble in water, so it disappears from view.
Sand is insoluble, so it does not dissolve.
The sand settles at the bottom of the glass.
example.answer: The salt dissolves; the sand settles at the bottom without dissolving.

learn.reallife: Windows use transparent glass to let light in, bathroom windows often use translucent frosted glass for privacy, and doors are opaque.

items.text: We cannot see through a wooden door because it is ___.

quiz.q: Which material is soluble in water?
quiz.explain: Sugar dissolves completely in water and disappears from view.
quiz.mistake: Thinks powders always dissolve

quiz.q: What happens when you pour a little cooking oil into water?
options: It forms a layer on top of the water
quiz.explain: Oil does not mix with water and floats as a separate layer.
quiz.mistake: Thinks all liquids mix with water

quiz.q: Which object will sink in water?
quiz.explain: An iron nail sinks, while a dry leaf, cork and thermocol float.
quiz.mistake: Thinks small objects always float

quiz.q: Butter paper lets you see objects only partly. It is:
quiz.explain: Translucent materials let some light through, so things look blurry.
quiz.mistake: Confuses translucent and transparent

quiz.q: Which material is opaque?
quiz.explain: We cannot see through cardboard at all, so it is opaque.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up opaque and transparent

quiz.q: Why are window panes usually made of clear glass?
options: Glass is transparent and lets light in
quiz.explain: Transparent glass lets light in and lets us see outside.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect transparency to the use of glass

quiz.q: A bathroom window uses frosted glass. Why?
options: It is opaque and blocks all light
It is transparent like clear glass
It lets light in but people cannot see clearly inside
quiz.explain: Frosted glass is translucent: light comes in, but you cannot see clearly through it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks translucent means blocking all light

quiz.q: Kiran stirs chalk powder in water and leaves it. What will she find after some time?
options: The chalk powder settles at the bottom
The chalk floats as a layer of oil
quiz.explain: Chalk is insoluble, so it does not dissolve and slowly settles down.
quiz.mistake: Thinks chalk dissolves like sugar

teach.ask: Gappu drops things into his water bowl: 'Sugar vanished, sand sank, and my leaf is sailing! Why?'
teach.praise: Wow! Sugar is soluble, sand is insoluble, and the leaf floats. And glass is transparent, butter paper translucent, wood opaque!
teach.nudge: Which things dissolve in water? And which ones float or sink?

learn.hook: If you had to build a kite, would you use paper or iron? Choosing the right material is a superpower!
points: We group materials by their properties: lustrous or dull, hard or soft, soluble or insoluble, floats or sinks, transparent, translucent or opaque.
Grouping helps us study materials and find what we need quickly.
We choose a material for a job based on its properties: glass for windows (transparent), iron for gates (hard and strong), cotton for summer clothes (soft and comfortable).
One material can belong to many groups: glass is transparent, hard and insoluble in water.
Reusing and recycling materials like paper, glass and metal saves resources.

example.q: Why are cooking pans usually made of metal and their handles of plastic or wood?
steps: A pan must get hot quickly and evenly to cook food; metals let heat pass through easily.
The handle must stay cool enough to hold safely.
Plastic and wood do not let heat pass through easily.
example.answer: Metal for the pan to heat the food; plastic or wood for the handle so it stays safe to hold.

learn.reallife: Potters choose soft wet clay to shape diyas and matkas, which become hard after baking. Builders choose hard bricks and stone for walls.

games.title: Pick the right material
pairs: cotton, because it is soft and comfortable
iron, because it is hard and strong

games.title: Grouping truths
items: Clear glass lets us see through and is difficult to scratch.
A material can belong to only one group.
One material can have many properties, like glass: transparent, hard and insoluble.
Grouping materials helps us choose the right one for a job.
Knowing properties helps us pick suitable materials.
Opaque materials are best for windows.
Windows need transparent materials to let light in.
Paper can be recycled to make new paper.
Recycling paper saves trees and resources.

quiz.q: Why do we group materials?
options: To study them easily and find what we need
quiz.explain: Grouping by properties makes it easier to compare materials and choose the right one.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the purpose of grouping

quiz.q: Which property makes glass good for windows?
quiz.explain: Transparent glass lets light and sight pass through.
quiz.mistake: Picks a property that does not matter for windows

quiz.q: Which group of materials is all transparent?
options: Butter paper, frosted glass, oiled paper
quiz.explain: We can see clearly through clear glass, clean water and air.
quiz.mistake: Confuses transparent with translucent or opaque

quiz.q: Which material is best for making a raincoat?
options: Plastic, because water does not pass through it
quiz.explain: Plastic does not let water through, which keeps you dry.
quiz.mistake: Does not match the property to the use

quiz.q: Glass is transparent, hard and does not dissolve in water. What does this show?
options: One material can belong to many groups
quiz.explain: Every material has many properties, so it fits into many groups at once.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a material fits only one group

quiz.q: Which of these objects is made of a material that is both lustrous and hard?
quiz.explain: A clean iron nail is shiny (lustrous) and hard.
quiz.mistake: Does not combine two properties

quiz.q: Why are diyas and matkas made from wet clay?
options: Wet clay is soft and easy to shape, and it becomes hard after baking
quiz.explain: Soft wet clay can be moulded into shapes. Once baked, it is hard and holds its shape.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect softness with shaping

quiz.q: Which material would you choose for a boat's float?
options: A material that sinks, like stone
A material that dissolves, like sugar
A material that floats, like wood or thermocol
quiz.explain: A float must stay on top of the water, so it needs a material that floats.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a property unrelated to floating

teach.ask: Gappu wants to build a nest-house: 'Should the window be wood or glass? How do people choose materials?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Look at the properties, group the materials, and choose the right one for the job: glass for my window!
teach.nudge: How do I decide which material to use? What should I look at?
